final.title: Rounding claims: when to keep it manual
final.body:
If you run a one-person business, the real question is not whether AI can “handle claims.” It is whether the work around claim rounding is repetitive enough to be a bounded workflow, instead of a fresh judgment call every time.

Use a simple decision rule. Keep it manual if each case needs new context, exceptions, or owner judgment. Consider support only if the same checks repeat and the rule can be written down clearly. In that narrower case, AI can sort, compare, or flag items before you review them. Final approval stays with you. Human-only approval and refusal of agent approval are demonstrated in Bareni’s self-built accounts-payable demo on synthetic data; for a claims workflow, that boundary is a design rule, not a deployed system.

The practical next step is to map one week of the current process. Write down the trigger, the inputs, the decision rule, where rounding happens, and where you stop to check by hand. Then note which part is actually repeatable. If the rule is stable, it may be a candidate for support. If it depends on judgment every time, manual review is still the right default.

Not every small-business workflow deserves automation. Sometimes the boring manual version is the correct one.

final.title: Rounding claims as a bounded workflow decision
final.body:
If you are running a one-person business, the useful question is not whether AI can “handle claims.” It is whether the rounding step is repeatable enough to treat as a bounded workflow instead of a fresh judgment call every time.

I would frame the choice like this: keep it manual if every case needs new context, exceptions, or owner judgment; consider support only for the narrow parts that repeat, such as sorting items, comparing fields, or flagging mismatches before you review them. Final approval stays with you. For money movement or other high-risk decisions, human approval is mandatory. In Bareni’s own synthetic accounts-payable demo, human-only approval and blocked agent payment attempts were demonstrated, but that is still a demo on synthetic data, not a claims system in production.

One practical next step is simple: map one week of the current process. Write down the trigger, the inputs, the rule you apply, where rounding happens, and where you stop to check by hand. Then mark the part that repeats most often. If the rule can be written clearly, it may be suitable for support. If it changes case by case, manual review is still the right default.

That is the filter: not “Can AI do it?” but “What is stable enough to standardise without handing over the decision?”
